RagShortTexts: The Hibernian faction is a module grouping, not proof of a united kingdom in 374.
Kin, cattle and reciprocal support shape local leadership; later law is not projected back.

Variants.Content: The module groups Hibernian communities into a faction, but fourth-century Ireland should not be treated as a single documented feudal monarchy. Local kin connections, cattle, land and armed followings provide a more cautious basis for political disputes than invented senatorial estates. Written evidence for this period is limited, and later Irish legal texts cannot be transferred intact into 374. Contacts across the sea can bring goods, captives and claims to prestige, while also exposing households to retaliation and absence of labour. A leader's standing depends on sustaining people and reciprocal obligations, not merely occupying a magnificent palace.

A man called to a sea expedition thinks about the boat, the weather and who will watch the animals while he is gone. A chief's promises must cover the return as well as departure. Plunder may enrich one following, but a wreck or retaliation leaves losses for the people who supplied the voyage and never boarded it.

A Hibernian leader builds support through kin and useful allies, yet obligations can pull in different directions. Lending men to a voyage may favour a partner while weakening protection at home. Later law books offer no ready answer to every dispute in 374; he needs an arrangement the households concerned will actually honour.
